stem: A 72-year-old woman gets chest pain and breathlessness when she hurries for a bus, and once felt faint on the stairs. Blood pressure is 124/88 mm Hg. Her ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy, and the second heart sound at the right upper sternal border is very soft.
oneliner: 72F + exertional chest pain, dyspnea, near-syncope + narrow pulse pressure + LVH on ECG + soft A2 → which murmur?
ask: Which auscultation finding is most likely?

options.A: Holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla
options.B: Early decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left sternal border
options.C: Opening snap followed by a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex
options.D: Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border
options.E: Holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration

whyNot.A: **Mitral regurgitation**: apical, no carotid radiation, and does not soften A2
whyNot.B: **Aortic regurgitation**: diastolic, with a **wide** pulse pressure; hers is narrow (124/88)
whyNot.C: **Mitral stenosis**: diastolic apical rumble, left atrial enlargement rather than LVH
whyNot.E: **Tricuspid regurgitation**: a right-sided lesion; it would not cause **LVH** or a soft A2

answer: Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, radiating to the carotids (aortic stenosis)
why: Angina, syncope and dyspnea on exertion with LVH point to **fixed outflow obstruction**. The murmur is **systolic, ejection-type, loudest at the right second intercostal space and carried to the carotids**, with a **soft S2** because the valve barely moves.

idea.rule: Aortic stenosis = ejection murmur to the neck, soft S2; the later the peak, the tighter the valve.
also: Pulsus parvus et tardus on the carotid
Paradoxically split S2 in severe disease
Murmur gets louder with squatting and softer with Valsalva
Triad: angina, syncope, dyspnea

stem: A 45-year-old man who drinks heavily every day has had three months of breathlessness lying flat and swollen ankles. He has a displaced, diffuse apical impulse and a third heart sound, and BNP is markedly raised.
oneliner: 45M + heavy alcohol + orthopnea + edema + S3 + displaced apex + raised BNP → which echo finding?
ask: Which echocardiographic finding is most likely?

options.A: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
options.B: Thick, echodense ventricular walls with normal cavity size and diastolic dysfunction
options.C: Thickened, calcified pericardium with normal ventricular function
options.D: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with normal ejection fraction
options.E: Dilated left ventricle with a low ejection fraction

whyNot.A: **Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy**: thick walls and a small cavity; her **displaced, diffuse apex and S3** mean a large dilated chamber
whyNot.B: **Infiltrative (amyloid) restrictive disease**: small cavity, low-voltage ECG; the stem has a displaced apex from a big ventricle
whyNot.C: **Constrictive pericarditis**: normal contractile function, no ventricular dilation or S3 from volume overload
whyNot.D: **Hypertensive heart disease**: no hypertension in the stem; a displaced diffuse apex means dilation, not thickening

answer: Dilated left ventricle with reduced ejection fraction (dilated cardiomyopathy)
why: Alcohol is a classic toxin causing **dilated cardiomyopathy**: **eccentric hypertrophy** with a big, thin-walled ventricle and **systolic failure**. The **S3** and **displaced diffuse apex** reflect the volume-loaded dilated chamber.

idea.rule: Dilated cardiomyopathy = big floppy ventricle, low EF, S3, cardiomegaly with pulmonary edema.
also: Causes: alcohol, doxorubicin, Coxsackie myocarditis, peripartum, Chagas, hemochromatosis
Chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary edema
Functional mitral regurgitation from annular stretch
Eccentric hypertrophy: sarcomeres added in series, so the chamber enlarges

stem: A 35-year-old woman raised abroad, who had repeated sore throats and a childhood illness with migrating joint pains, develops new palpitations and breathlessness that is worse during her pregnancy. ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm.
oneliner: 35F + childhood rheumatic fever + dyspnea worse in pregnancy + new AF → which murmur?
ask: Which auscultation finding is most likely?

options.A: Opening snap followed by a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex
options.B: Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space
options.C: Holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla
options.D: Midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur
options.E: Fixed, widely split S2 with a pulmonic flow murmur

whyNot.B: **Aortic stenosis**: a systolic murmur; rheumatic disease scars the **mitral** valve first, and her AF points to an enlarged left atrium
whyNot.C: **Mitral regurgitation**: systolic; tachycardia and pregnancy worsen **stenosis** by shortening diastole, not regurgitation
whyNot.D: **Mitral valve prolapse**: a myxomatous, not rheumatic, lesion; it does not worsen with the shorter diastole of pregnancy
whyNot.E: **Atrial septal defect**: no rheumatic link, and the split S2 does not explain symptoms worse with fast heart rate

answer: Opening snap and mid-diastolic rumble at the apex (mitral stenosis)
why: Rheumatic fever scars the mitral valve into a **fixed narrow orifice**. Blood crossing it in diastole gives an **opening snap** then a **low-pitched rumble**; **tachycardia and pregnancy** shorten diastole and raise left atrial pressure, so the **left atrium enlarges and AF** follows.

idea.rule: Mitral stenosis = diastolic apical rumble after an opening snap; shorter OS-S2 gap means tighter valve.
also: Left atrial enlargement causes AF and thrombus
Dysphagia or hoarseness from a large left atrium (Ortner syndrome)
Murmur louder in left lateral position and on expiration
Almost always rheumatic in origin

stem: A 60-year-old man has had slowly worsening breathlessness on exertion over several years. Echocardiography shows a dilated left atrium, a mildly enlarged left ventricle with normal wall thickness, normal right heart chambers, mitral leaflets that open widely in diastole, and a normal aortic valve.
oneliner: 60M + slow exertional dyspnea + big left atrium + mildly big LV, normal walls + mitral leaflets open widely + normal aortic valve → which murmur?
ask: Which auscultation finding is most likely?

options.A: Early decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left sternal border
options.B: Low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex after a snap
options.C: Blowing holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
options.D: Crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids
options.E: Holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration

whyNot.A: **Aortic regurgitation**: needs a diseased aortic valve; his **aortic valve is normal**
whyNot.B: **Mitral stenosis**: also a big left atrium, but his **mitral leaflets open widely**
whyNot.D: **Aortic stenosis**: needs a diseased aortic valve and thick LV walls; his valve and wall thickness are **normal**
whyNot.E: **Tricuspid regurgitation**: enlarges the right heart; his **right chambers are normal**

answer: Holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla (mitral regurgitation)
why: Blood leaks back into the left atrium throughout **systole**, giving a **blowing holosystolic apical murmur to the axilla**. Years of volume load **enlarge the left atrium** and dilate the ventricle without thickening its walls, while **normal leaflet opening** and a **normal aortic valve** exclude the other left-sided lesions.

idea.rule: Mitral regurgitation = holosystolic apical murmur to the axilla, with a big left atrium.
also: Causes: prolapse, rheumatic disease, endocarditis, papillary muscle rupture after MI
Louder with handgrip or squatting
S3 appears when the ventricle fails
Acute MR: soft murmur and pulmonary edema, little atrial enlargement

stem: A 19-year-old male athlete collapsed during a sprint. His father died suddenly at 40. Between episodes he has no breathlessness and his lungs are clear. A systolic murmur is louder when he stands up and softer when he squats.
oneliner: 19M + exertional syncope + FH sudden death + murmur louder standing, softer squatting → which carotid pulse?
ask: Which carotid pulse finding is most likely?

options.A: Pulsus parvus et tardus
options.B: Pulsus alternans
options.C: Pulsus paradoxus
options.D: Bisferiens (bifid) pulse
options.E: Water-hammer pulse

whyNot.A: **Aortic stenosis**: slow, weak upstroke, and its murmur **softens** on standing; his grows louder
whyNot.B: **Severe LV systolic failure**: alternating strong and weak beats; he has no breathlessness and clear lungs
whyNot.C: **Tamponade or severe asthma**: inspiratory fall in pressure; nothing in the stem suggests either
whyNot.E: **Aortic regurgitation**: a diastolic murmur that softens on standing; his murmur is systolic and grows on standing

answer: Bifid carotid pulse (hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy)
why: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy gives a **murmur that grows with less preload (standing, Valsalva)**. Early rapid ejection, then **mid-systolic obstruction** by the septum and anterior mitral leaflet, and a second wave produce the **two-peaked pulse**.

idea.rule: Bifid pulse = fast ejection, mid-systolic outflow obstruction, then a second peak (HOCM, or AR).
also: Aortic regurgitation can also give a bisferiens pulse
Murmur softens with squatting, handgrip, passive leg raise
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion on echo
Sudden death in young athletes

stem: A 58-year-old man has had an hour of crushing chest pain. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with ST elevation in the inferior leads. His lungs are clear, the jugular venous pressure is normal, chest x-ray shows a normal heart size, and no murmur is heard. An extra heart sound is present.
oneliner: 58M + 1 h crushing chest pain + inferior ST elevation, sinus rhythm + clear lungs + normal heart size + no murmur + extra sound → which sound?
ask: Which extra heart sound is most likely?

options.A: S3 gallop
options.B: S4 gallop
options.C: Opening snap
options.D: Pericardial knock
options.E: Fixed splitting of S2

whyNot.A: **Rapid filling of a dilated, failing ventricle**; his heart size is normal and lungs clear
whyNot.C: **Mitral stenosis** gives a snap followed by a diastolic rumble; **no murmur** is heard
whyNot.D: **Constrictive pericarditis**, a chronic illness with raised JVP; his JVP is **normal**
whyNot.E: **Atrial septal defect**, a chronic shunt with a flow murmur; **no murmur** here, and it does not arise with an acute infarct

answer: S4 (atrial contraction into a stiff, ischemic ventricle)
why: Ischemia makes the ventricle **stiff and non-compliant**, so the atrial contraction into it vibrates as an **S4**, heard **just before S1**. He is in **sinus rhythm** (an atrial kick is present) and the ventricle is **not dilated or failing**, so an S3 is not expected.

idea.rule: S4 = atrial kick into a stiff ventricle (late diastole, before S1); S3 = rapid filling of a dilated one.
also: Left ventricular hypertrophy
Hypertensive heart disease
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Absent in atrial fibrillation (no atrial kick)

stem: A 41-year-old woman has new hypertension that remains high on three drugs. An abdominal bruit is heard and her serum potassium is low. Her creatinine rose after an ACE inhibitor was added.
oneliner: 41F + resistant hypertension + abdominal bruit + low K+ + creatinine rise on ACE inhibitor → which hormone and electrolyte pattern?
ask: Which pattern of renin, aldosterone and acid-base state is most likely?

options.A: Low renin, high aldosterone, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis
options.B: Low renin, low aldosterone, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis
options.C: High renin, high aldosterone, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis
options.D: High renin, low aldosterone, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis
options.E: Low renin, low aldosterone, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis

whyNot.A: **Primary hyperaldosteronism**: renin is suppressed; her bruit and creatinine rise on an ACE inhibitor show **renal hypoperfusion driving renin up**
whyNot.B: **Liddle syndrome or mineralocorticoid excess**: both hormones low; a stenotic kidney would **raise** renin
whyNot.D: **Primary adrenal insufficiency** pattern; she is **hypokalemic**
whyNot.E: **Hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism (type 4 RTA)**; she is **hypokalemic** and the stenotic kidney raises renin

answer: High renin and aldosterone with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
why: A narrowed renal artery makes the kidney sense **low perfusion**, so it releases **renin**. Angiotensin II raises **aldosterone**, which wastes **K+ and H+**, giving **hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis**. When filtration depends on angiotensin II (bilateral stenosis or a single kidney), an ACE inhibitor drops glomerular pressure, hence the **creatinine rise**.

idea.rule: Renal artery stenosis = secondary hyperaldosteronism: renin up, aldosterone up, K+ down.
also: Fibromuscular dysplasia in young women (string of beads)
Atherosclerotic stenosis in older smokers
Renin-secreting juxtaglomerular tumor: renin up, aldosterone up, K+ down
Diuretic use or heart failure (low effective volume) gives the same high-renin pattern

stem: A 3-month-old boy sweats and tires during feeds and has gained little weight. Oxygen saturation is 98% in the right hand and the foot, and femoral pulses are strong. At cardiac catheterization, oxygen saturation rises between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
oneliner: 3-month-old boy + tires and sweats with feeds + poor weight gain + normal saturation + strong femorals + O2 step-up RA→RV → which murmur?
ask: Which auscultation finding is most likely?

options.A: Fixed, widely split S2 with a systolic ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border
options.B: Continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle
options.C: Holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla
options.D: Systolic ejection murmur below the left clavicle with weak femoral pulses
options.E: Harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border

whyNot.A: **Atrial septal defect**: the oxygen step-up would be in the **right atrium**, not between atrium and ventricle
whyNot.B: **Patent ductus arteriosus**: the step-up would be in the **pulmonary artery**
whyNot.C: **Mitral regurgitation**: no left-to-right shunt, so no oxygen step-up in the right heart
whyNot.D: **Coarctation**: weak femoral pulses; his are **strong**, and there is no shunt

answer: Holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border (ventricular septal defect)
why: A **ventricular septal defect** shunts blood from the high-pressure left ventricle to the right throughout systole, giving a **harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border**. The **left-to-right shunt** causes heart failure symptoms in infants but **no cyanosis**.

idea.rule: VSD = harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border; a small hole is louder than a big one.
also: Most common congenital heart defect
Eisenmenger syndrome if untreated: murmur disappears, late cyanosis
Associated with fetal alcohol syndrome and trisomies
Many small muscular defects close on their own

stem: A 70-year-old woman with pyelonephritis is confused. Temperature is 39.2°C, pulse is 124/min, and blood pressure is 78/38 mm Hg despite a large saline bolus. Her hands are warm and flushed, and capillary refill is brisk. A central line and pulmonary artery catheter are placed.
oneliner: 70F + pyelonephritis + fever + tachycardia + hypotension unresponsive to fluids + warm, flushed hands → which hemodynamic values?
ask: Which set of hemodynamic values is most likely?

options.A: CVP high, PCWP high, cardiac output low, SVR high
options.B: CVP low, PCWP low, cardiac output low, SVR high
options.C: CVP low, PCWP low, cardiac output low, SVR low
options.D: CVP high, PCWP low, cardiac output low, SVR high
options.E: CVP low, PCWP low, cardiac output high, SVR low

whyNot.A: **Cardiogenic shock**: vasoconstricted, cool periphery; her hands are **warm and flushed**
whyNot.B: **Hypovolemic shock**: high SVR gives cool skin with slow refill; hers is **warm with brisk refill**
whyNot.C: **Neurogenic shock**: vasodilation with **bradycardia** after cord injury; she has an infection and a pulse of **124**
whyNot.D: **Massive pulmonary embolism**: right heart pressure rises and the skin is cool; her hands are **warm**

answer: Low CVP and PCWP, high cardiac output, low SVR (early septic, distributive shock)
why: In early sepsis **cytokines and nitric oxide dilate vessels**, so **SVR falls** and filling pressures (**CVP, PCWP**) drop. Tachycardia and low afterload **raise cardiac output**, which is why the skin is **warm and flushed with brisk refill** despite hypotension.

idea.rule: Distributive shock: SVR down, filling pressures down, cardiac output up, warm periphery; cardiogenic/hypovolemic: SVR up, cool skin.
also: Anaphylaxis
Neurogenic shock (but with bradycardia and low output)
Adrenal crisis
Late sepsis can turn cool as output falls

stem: A 60-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension has sudden tearing chest pain that radiates between his shoulder blades. Blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg in the right arm and 135/70 mm Hg in the left. Heart sounds are crisp and the lungs are clear.
oneliner: 60M + HTN + sudden tearing chest pain to the back + arm BP difference → which imaging finding?
ask: Which imaging finding is most likely?

options.A: Wedge-shaped peripheral opacity on chest CT
options.B: Widened mediastinum, with an intimal flap on CT angiography
options.C: Water-bottle-shaped cardiac silhouette with clear lungs
options.D: Pneumoperitoneum under the right hemidiaphragm
options.E: Egg-on-a-string cardiac silhouette

whyNot.A: **Pulmonary infarct** from PE: does not give tearing pain to the back with a **45 mm Hg gap between the arms**
whyNot.C: **Large pericardial effusion**: muffled heart sounds; his are **crisp**, and it does not cause unequal arm pressures
whyNot.D: **Perforated viscus**: abdominal pain with peritonitis, not tearing chest pain to the back
whyNot.E: **Transposition** of the great arteries: a cyanotic newborn, not a 60-year-old with chest pain

answer: Widened mediastinum on x-ray; intimal flap separating true and false lumens
why: Blood entering a tear in the intima **dissects the media**, creating a **false lumen** that compresses branch vessels (hence the **arm pressure difference**). Chest x-ray shows a **widened mediastinum**; **CT angiography or TEE** shows the **intimal flap**.

idea.rule: Dissection = tearing pain to the back + unequal arm BPs + wide mediastinum + intimal flap.
also: Risks: hypertension, Marfan syndrome, bicuspid valve, cocaine
Complications: aortic regurgitation, tamponade, limb or renal ischemia
Type A (ascending) is surgical; type B (descending) is medical
Cystic medial degeneration

stem: An 8-year-old boy has headaches and a blood pressure of 150/90 mm Hg in his right arm. He complains of cold feet and tires during games. Oxygen saturation is normal. A soft systolic murmur is heard over his back.
oneliner: 8M + headaches + arm hypertension + cold feet + tires on exertion + murmur over the back → which physical finding?
ask: Which physical finding is most likely?

options.A: Weak femoral pulses that lag behind the radial pulse
options.B: Higher blood pressure in the legs than in the arms
options.C: Fixed, widely split S2 with a pulmonic flow murmur
options.D: Continuous murmur below the left clavicle with bounding pulses
options.E: Cyanosis of the lower limbs with pink upper limbs

whyNot.B: Leg pressure slightly above arm pressure is the **normal** pattern; arm hypertension with **cold feet** points to obstruction between them
whyNot.C: **Atrial septal defect**: no hypertension or cold limbs
whyNot.D: **Patent ductus arteriosus**: bounding, not diminished, pulses and no differential pressure
whyNot.E: **Differential cyanosis** from PDA with reversed flow; his **oxygen saturation is normal**

answer: Weak, delayed femoral pulses (radiofemoral delay); arm pressure above leg pressure (coarctation)
why: A narrowing of the aorta near the ductus gives **hypertension proximal** to it and **poor perfusion distal** to it: **weak, delayed femoral pulses**, **cold feet** and an **arm-leg pressure gradient**. Collaterals through intercostal arteries produce the back murmur.

idea.rule: Coarctation = arm BP higher than leg BP with radiofemoral delay.
also: Associated with Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve
Rib notching on x-ray from intercostal collaterals
Infantile type is preductal and ductus-dependent
Complication: berry aneurysm rupture, aortic dissection

stem: A 62-year-old man is readmitted 4 days after an anterior myocardial infarction with new chest pain and fresh ST elevation. Troponin I is still raised from the first event. The team asks which cardiac marker can best show whether a new infarct has occurred.
oneliner: 62M + 4 days post-MI + new chest pain + ST elevation + troponin raised → which marker property helps?
ask: Which statement about cardiac markers best fits this situation?

options.A: CK-MB normalises in 2-3 days, so a new rise means reinfarction
options.B: Troponin I falls to normal within 24 hours of infarction
options.C: Myoglobin is the most specific marker of cardiac necrosis
options.D: LDH rises within 1 hour of the infarct and peaks early
options.E: CK-MB stays raised for 10 days after infarction

whyNot.B: Troponin stays raised **7-10 days**, which is why it is unhelpful here and the stem notes it is still raised
whyNot.C: Myoglobin is **the earliest but least specific**; it also leaks from skeletal muscle
whyNot.D: LDH rises late, after **24-48 hours**, and is not used now
whyNot.E: That describes **troponin**; CK-MB is gone in about 2-3 days

answer: CK-MB: rises in 4-6 hours, normal by 2-3 days, useful for reinfarction
why: **CK-MB** rises within about **4-6 hours** of myocyte necrosis and **returns to normal in 2-3 days**. Troponin stays up for 7-10 days, so after 4 days a **fresh CK-MB rise** points to a new infarct (in practice a further rise in troponin of over 20% is also used).

idea.rule: Troponin = long-lasting, specific; CK-MB = short-lived, reinfarction marker.
also: Troponin I or T: rises 3-4 h, stays up 7-10 days, so it cannot date a second event easily
Myoglobin is earliest but nonspecific
LDH was the old late marker (rises at 24-48 h)
A rising and falling pattern separates MI from chronic troponin elevation

stem: A newborn boy of a mother with poorly controlled pregestational diabetes becomes deeply blue during the first day of life. No murmur is heard. The cyanosis does not improve after breathing 100% oxygen, and worsens when the ductus begins to close.
oneliner: Newborn boy + diabetic mother + cyanosis on day 1 + no murmur + no response to 100% O2 + worse as ductus closes → which chest x-ray finding?
ask: Which chest x-ray finding is most likely?

options.A: Boot-shaped heart with reduced lung markings
options.B: Snowman (figure-of-eight) heart silhouette
options.C: Notching of the lower borders of the ribs
options.D: Egg-on-a-string heart with a narrow pedicle
options.E: Water-bottle-shaped cardiac silhouette

whyNot.A: **Tetralogy of Fallot**: right outflow stenosis gives a loud systolic murmur; **no murmur** is heard here
whyNot.B: **Supracardiac TAPVR**: mixing is at the atrial level, so closing the **ductus** would not worsen it
whyNot.C: **Coarctation** in an older child: hypertension and weak leg pulses, not cyanosis on day 1
whyNot.E: **Pericardial effusion**: not a cause of cyanosis on the first day

answer: Egg-on-a-string heart (transposition of the great arteries)
why: The **aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left**, so two parallel circuits keep blue blood in the body. Survival depends on **mixing through the ductus or foramen**, hence **worsening as it closes**. X-ray shows an **egg-on-a-string** heart with a narrow mediastinum.

idea.rule: TGA = parallel circuits, cyanosis at birth, no response to oxygen; mixing keeps the baby alive.
also: Treat with prostaglandin E1 to keep the ductus open
Maternal diabetes is a risk factor
Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
Surgical arterial switch

stem: A 41-year-old woman has hypertension, low serum potassium and a bruit over the right upper abdomen. Arteriography shows a narrowed right renal artery, a smaller right kidney and a normal left renal artery. Renal vein samples are taken from each side.
oneliner: 41F + HTN + hypokalemia + right abdominal bruit + narrow right renal artery, normal left + smaller right kidney → which renal vein renin pattern?
ask: Which renal vein renin pattern is most likely?

options.A: Equal high renin in both veins
options.B: Low renin in both veins
options.C: Left vein high, right vein low
options.D: Right vein high, left vein suppressed
options.E: Right vein normal, left vein high

whyNot.A: **Bilateral stenosis**; here only the **right** artery is narrowed and the **left artery is normal**
whyNot.B: **Primary hyperaldosteronism**-type suppression; the stenotic kidney would still release renin
whyNot.C: The **reverse**: the ischemic right kidney is the one that senses low perfusion
whyNot.E: The healthy left kidney is **suppressed** by the high angiotensin II, not raised

answer: Renin high from the stenotic kidney and suppressed from the normal kidney
why: The **stenotic** kidney sees low perfusion and **releases renin**. The rising angiotensin II and volume retention **suppress renin from the opposite, normal kidney**. A **high-to-low ratio** across the two renal veins **lateralises** the lesion.

idea.rule: Unilateral stenosis: the narrowed side makes renin; the healthy side switches off.
also: A renal vein renin ratio of about 1.5 or more lateralises the lesion
Captopril raises renin further from the stenotic kidney
Renin-secreting tumor: renin high from the tumor side, suppressed from the other
Atrophy of the affected kidney from low flow

stem: A 40-year-old man who has lived at high altitude for two years has breathlessness, a raised jugular venous pressure and ankle swelling. A parasternal heave is felt and the pulmonary component of the second heart sound is loud.
oneliner: 40M + 2 yr at high altitude + dyspnea + raised JVP + edema + parasternal heave + loud P2 → which ECG finding?
ask: Which ECG finding is most likely?

options.A: Left axis deviation with tall R waves in V5-V6
options.B: Broad notched P waves in lead II
options.C: Low voltage with electrical alternans
options.D: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression
options.E: Right axis deviation with a tall R wave in V1

whyNot.A: **Left ventricular hypertrophy**: the stem has right-sided signs (heave, loud P2, raised JVP)
whyNot.B: **P mitrale** of left atrial enlargement; his signs are right-sided, and right atrial strain gives tall **peaked** P waves
whyNot.C: **Large pericardial effusion**: muffled sounds; his **P2 is loud** and a heave is felt
whyNot.D: **Acute pericarditis**: acute chest pain; he has **chronic** right-sided overload with no pain

answer: Right axis deviation and tall R in V1 (right ventricular hypertrophy)
why: Chronic hypoxia causes **pulmonary vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension**, so the right ventricle hypertrophies (**cor pulmonale**). The ECG shows **right axis deviation** and a **dominant R in V1**, with possible **peaked P waves** from right atrial strain.

idea.rule: Right-sided pressure overload = right axis, tall R in V1, peaked P in II.
also: COPD and chronic hypoxia
Pulmonary embolism: S1Q3T3
Eisenmenger syndrome
Left atrial enlargement gives broad P waves instead

stem: A 21-year-old woman has fatigue and breathlessness on exertion. The second heart sound is widely split and does not change with breathing. A soft systolic flow murmur is heard at the upper left sternal border.
oneliner: 21F + fatigue + exertional dyspnea + fixed wide-split S2 + soft flow murmur upper left sternal border → which ECG finding?
ask: Which ECG finding is most likely?

options.A: Left axis deviation with LVH voltage
options.B: Right axis deviation with incomplete RBBB
options.C: Delta wave with a short PR interval
options.D: Low voltage with electrical alternans
options.E: Left bundle branch block with a wide QRS

whyNot.A: LVH fits pressure load on the **left** ventricle; a fixed split S2 with a flow murmur means **right-sided volume load**
whyNot.C: **Pre-excitation (WPW)**: an accessory pathway does not cause a **fixed split S2** or a flow murmur
whyNot.D: **Pericardial effusion**: muffles heart sounds; it does not give a **fixed split S2**
whyNot.E: **LBBB** delays A2 and gives **paradoxical** splitting, not fixed splitting

answer: Right axis deviation and incomplete RBBB (secundum atrial septal defect)
why: The **fixed split S2** shows a **left-to-right shunt at atrial level**. The right heart carries extra blood, so the ECG shows **right axis deviation** and **incomplete right bundle branch block** from RV volume overload.

idea.rule: ASD = fixed split S2 + RV volume load: right axis, RBBB pattern, flow murmur.
also: Right bundle branch block also widens S2 (but the split still varies with breathing)
Pulmonary stenosis: wide split from delayed P2
Ostium primum ASD instead gives left axis deviation (AV canal)
Late: pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger

stem: A 74-year-old woman with hypertension reports palpitations. Today she has sudden weakness of the right arm and leg and difficulty speaking. Her pulse is completely irregular in both rhythm and volume.
oneliner: 74F + hypertension + palpitations + sudden right-sided weakness + irregularly irregular pulse → which ECG finding?
ask: Which ECG finding is most likely?

options.A: Sawtooth flutter waves at a regular rate
options.B: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no discrete P waves
options.C: P waves with no relation to QRS complexes
options.D: Progressive PR lengthening until a beat is dropped
options.E: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia with hidden P waves

whyNot.A: **Atrial flutter**: usually a **regular** rate with fixed block; her pulse is completely irregular
whyNot.C: **Third-degree block**: a slow, **regular** escape rhythm; her pulse is completely irregular
whyNot.D: **Mobitz I** gives a regularly irregular, grouped pattern, not chaotic
whyNot.E: **AVNRT**: regular and paroxysmal, with no embolic risk by itself

answer: Irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves (atrial fibrillation)
why: The atria fire chaotically, so there are **no discrete P waves** and the AV node conducts **randomly**, giving an **irregularly irregular** rhythm. Stasis in the **left atrial appendage** forms thrombi that embolise to the brain.

idea.rule: AF = irregularly irregular, no P waves, risk of cardioembolic stroke.
also: Causes: hypertension, mitral stenosis, hyperthyroidism, alcohol
Anticoagulate by CHA2DS2-VASc
Absent a wave in the JVP
Rate or rhythm control with beta blockers, amiodarone, cardioversion

stem: An 80-year-old woman with heart failure takes digoxin and a loop diuretic, and her kidney function has recently worsened. Her serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L, and a new irregular rhythm is detected on the monitor.
oneliner: 80F + digoxin + loop diuretic + worsening renal function + K+ 3.0 + new arrhythmia → which symptoms?
ask: Which set of symptoms is she most likely to report?

options.A: Gingival hyperplasia and peripheral edema
options.B: Dry cough and angioedema of the lips
options.C: Flushing, headache and reflex tachycardia
options.D: Anorexia, nausea and blurred or yellow vision
options.E: Blue-gray skin and corneal deposits

whyNot.A: **Phenytoin or calcium channel blocker** effects; she takes neither
whyNot.B: **ACE inhibitor** effects; she takes digoxin and a loop diuretic
whyNot.C: **Nitrate or dihydropyridine** effects; she takes neither
whyNot.E: **Amiodarone** effects; she is not taking it

answer: Gastrointestinal upset with blurred/yellow vision (digoxin toxicity)
why: Digoxin is cleared by the kidneys, so **renal impairment** raises levels; **low potassium** from the loop diuretic worsens toxicity because digoxin binds the Na+/K+ pump more when K+ is low. Toxicity gives **anorexia, nausea, vomiting, blurred or yellow vision** and **arrhythmias**.

idea.rule: Digoxin toxicity = GI upset + yellow vision + arrhythmia; worse with renal failure and low K+.
also: Hyperkalemia in acute overdose (pump blocked in all cells)
Verapamil, amiodarone and quinidine raise digoxin levels
Low magnesium also increases toxicity
Treat with digoxin-specific antibody Fab fragments

stem: A 49-year-old woman has a strong family history of early coronary disease. She has no tendon xanthomas. Relatives show different lipid phenotypes: some with high LDL, some with high triglycerides, and some with both.
oneliner: 49F + premature CAD in family + no tendon xanthomas + relatives with varied high LDL and/or TG → which lipid pattern?
ask: Which lipid pattern is most likely in her?

options.A: Isolated very high LDL with normal triglycerides
options.B: Very high triglycerides with chylomicrons and normal LDL
options.C: Raised LDL and raised triglycerides
options.D: Raised IDL remnants with low or normal LDL
options.E: Very low LDL with fat malabsorption

whyNot.A: **Familial hypercholesterolemia**: tendon xanthomas and normal triglycerides; she has **no xanthomas** and relatives have high TG
whyNot.B: **Lipoprotein lipase or apoC-II deficiency**: raises chylomicrons, not LDL; her relatives have **high LDL**
whyNot.D: **Dysbetalipoproteinemia (apoE2)**: remnants, not LDL, are raised; relatives with **isolated high LDL** do not fit
whyNot.E: **Abetalipoproteinemia**: LDL is absent; her relatives have **high LDL** and early CAD

answer: Raised LDL and triglycerides (familial combined hyperlipidemia)
why: **Familial combined hyperlipidemia** (autosomal dominant, **overproduction of VLDL**) gives **high LDL and triglycerides**, often varying within a family, and premature CAD. **No tendon xanthomas** distinguishes it from familial hypercholesterolemia.

idea.rule: Read the family pattern: LDL and TG both up, varying between relatives, no xanthomas = familial combined hyperlipidemia.
also: Familial hypercholesterolemia: LDL alone, tendon xanthomas
Dysbetalipoproteinemia: apoE2, raised remnants, palmar xanthomas
LPL deficiency: chylomicrons, pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas
Familial hypertriglyceridemia: VLDL alone

stem: A 45-year-old man with a blood pressure of 240/140 mm Hg has a severe headache and blurred vision. His urinalysis shows hematuria and his creatinine is raised. An ophthalmoscope is used to look at his retina.
oneliner: 45M + BP 240/140 + headache + blurred vision + hematuria + raised creatinine → which fundus finding?
ask: Which fundus finding is most likely?

options.A: Cherry-red spot at the macula with a pale retina
options.B: Neovascularization with microaneurysms and dot-blot hemorrhages
options.C: Flame hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and papilledema
options.D: Roth spots with an otherwise normal retina
options.E: Normal fundus with a relative afferent pupillary defect

whyNot.A: **Central retinal artery occlusion**: sudden one-eye loss of vision; it does not explain **BP 240/140 with kidney injury**
whyNot.B: **Diabetic retinopathy**: diabetes is not given, and it does not explain **BP 240/140 with acute kidney injury**
whyNot.D: **Roth spots** of endocarditis; they do not explain **BP 240/140 with kidney injury**
whyNot.E: **Optic neuritis**: affects the optic nerve alone; it does not explain **BP 240/140 with kidney injury**

answer: Flame hemorrhages, arteriolar narrowing, cotton-wool spots, papilledema
why: Hypertensive emergency means **severe hypertension with end-organ damage** (eye, kidney, brain). The retina shows **flame hemorrhages**, **cotton-wool spots** and **papilledema**, and the kidney shows **hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (onion-skin)**.

idea.rule: Hypertensive emergency = very high BP + organ damage; fundus shows hemorrhages, exudates, papilledema.
also: Malignant nephrosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis
Hypertensive encephalopathy
Lower mean pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour
Use IV labetalol, nicardipine or clevidipine

stem: An 80-year-old woman, who has no symptoms and exercises daily, has a soft early-peaking systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border on a routine visit. The murmur softens with the Valsalva maneuver. Her carotid pulse rises briskly and A2 is of normal intensity.
oneliner: 80F + asymptomatic + soft early-peaking systolic murmur at RUSB + softer with Valsalva + brisk carotids + normal A2 → which echo finding?
ask: Which echocardiographic finding is most likely?

options.A: Calcified aortic valve with a large systolic pressure gradient
options.B: Thickened aortic leaflets with no significant pressure gradient
options.C: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion
options.D: Myxomatous mitral leaflet prolapsing into the left atrium
options.E: Dilated left ventricle with a low ejection fraction

whyNot.A: **Aortic stenosis**: a gradient slows the carotid upstroke and softens A2; hers are **brisk and normal**
whyNot.C: **Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy**: murmur grows with Valsalva; hers **softens**
whyNot.D: **Mitral valve prolapse**: an apical click and late murmur; hers is at the **right upper sternal border**
whyNot.E: **Dilated cardiomyopathy**: heart failure symptoms; she is **asymptomatic** and exercises daily

answer: Thickened aortic leaflets without a pressure gradient (aortic sclerosis)
why: **Aortic sclerosis** is leaflet thickening **without outflow obstruction**, so there is **no pressure gradient**. The **carotid upstroke and A2 stay normal** and the murmur peaks early, unlike stenosis.

idea.rule: Sclerosis = murmur only; stenosis = murmur plus slow pulse, soft S2, symptoms.
also: Common in the elderly
No pressure gradient on echo
Risk factors same as atherosclerosis
Peak later = more severe stenosis

stem: A 16-year-old thin girl has occasional palpitations and is otherwise well. Her examination is normal except for a late systolic murmur at the apex that starts earlier when she stands and later when she squats.
oneliner: 16F + thin + occasional palpitations + late systolic apical murmur, earlier on standing, later on squatting → which extra sound?
ask: Which extra sound is most likely heard just before this murmur?

options.A: Midsystolic click
options.B: Opening snap
options.C: Aortic ejection click
options.D: Pericardial knock
options.E: Tumor plop

whyNot.B: **Mitral stenosis**: a diastolic sound; her murmur is **systolic**
whyNot.C: **Bicuspid aortic valve**: early systolic at the **base**, and it does not shift with standing
whyNot.D: **Constrictive pericarditis**: an early diastolic sound; her murmur is **systolic**
whyNot.E: **Atrial myxoma**: a diastolic sound; her murmur is **systolic**

answer: Midsystolic click and late systolic murmur (mitral valve prolapse)
why: A floppy **myxomatous** mitral leaflet **prolapses into the left atrium** in mid-systole and snaps tight, causing the **click**. **Less preload (standing, Valsalva)** makes the ventricle smaller so prolapse occurs **earlier**.

idea.rule: MVP = midsystolic click that moves earlier with decreased preload.
also: Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes
Myxomatous degeneration
Usually benign
Can progress to mitral regurgitation

stem: A 25-year-old healthy man has a routine ECG before being cleared for sports. The tracing is normal, with a regular rhythm.
oneliner: 25M + healthy + routine ECG + normal tracing → which interval values?
ask: Which pair of interval values is expected on this ECG?

options.A: PR 80 ms, QRS 90 ms
options.B: PR 250 ms, QRS 90 ms
options.C: PR 160 ms, QRS 90 ms
options.D: PR 160 ms, QRS 140 ms
options.E: PR 90 ms, QRS 140 ms

whyNot.A: A **short PR** suggests an accessory pathway (WPW), not a normal tracing
whyNot.B: A **prolonged PR** over 200 ms is **first-degree AV block**
whyNot.D: A QRS over 120 ms means **bundle branch block**
whyNot.E: Both abnormal: short PR and a **wide QRS**

answer: PR 120-200 ms, QRS under 120 ms
why: The **PR interval** (120-200 ms) covers atrial depolarisation plus the **AV nodal delay**, which accounts for most of it. A **normal QRS is under 120 ms**, reflecting fast His-Purkinje conduction.

idea.rule: PR 120-200 ms (mostly AV node delay); QRS under 120 ms.
also: Prolonged PR = first-degree block
Short PR = pre-excitation
Wide QRS = bundle branch block or ventricular origin
AV node delay allows ventricular filling

stem: A 70-year-old man with heart failure has orthopnea, a raised JVP and a third heart sound. Dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds are found at both lung bases. A thoracentesis is performed.
oneliner: 70M + heart failure + orthopnea + raised JVP + S3 + bibasilar dullness → which effusion type?
ask: Which pleural effusion type is most likely?

options.A: Unilateral exudate with low glucose
options.B: Bloody exudate with malignant cells
options.C: Milky effusion with high triglycerides
options.D: Purulent fluid with low pH
options.E: Bilateral transudate with low protein

whyNot.A: **Rheumatoid or tuberculous** effusion: one-sided, high protein
whyNot.B: **Malignancy**: the signs here fit a systemic congestive state, not a unilateral mass
whyNot.C: **Chylothorax** from thoracic duct injury or lymphoma; his findings are those of **venous congestion** (raised JVP, S3)
whyNot.D: **Empyema**: fever and pneumonia, not bilateral dullness with S3

answer: Bilateral transudate (heart failure)
why: Raised **hydrostatic pressure** in the pulmonary and systemic veins pushes **low-protein fluid** into the pleura on both sides, giving a **transudate**. A **raised JVP and S3** fit systemic congestion, and effusions improve with **diuretics**.

idea.rule: Raised venous pressure = bilateral transudate; infection or tumour = exudate.
also: Cirrhosis: transudative hepatic hydrothorax
Nephrotic syndrome (low oncotic pressure)
Light criteria separate transudate from exudate
Right-sided effusion is often larger in HF

stem: A 68-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy has a third heart sound and a raised jugular venous pressure. Echocardiography shows structurally normal mitral leaflets and a normal aortic valve. His murmur lessens after diuretic treatment.
oneliner: 68M + dilated cardiomyopathy + S3 + raised JVP + normal mitral leaflets + normal aortic valve + murmur improves with diuresis → which murmur?
ask: Which murmur is most likely?

options.A: Holosystolic murmur at the apex
options.B: Crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the right base
options.C: Mid-diastolic rumble after an opening snap
options.D: Midsystolic click with a late murmur
options.E: Continuous machine-like murmur

whyNot.B: **Aortic stenosis**: needs a diseased aortic valve; his is **normal**
whyNot.C: **Mitral stenosis**: rheumatic leaflets, not normal here
whyNot.D: **Mitral valve prolapse**: floppy leaflets, not normal ones
whyNot.E: **Patent ductus arteriosus**: a duct, not ventricular size, causes it, so diuresis would not change it

answer: Holosystolic apical murmur (functional mitral regurgitation)
why: A **dilated left ventricle stretches the mitral annulus** and pulls the papillary muscles outward, so structurally normal leaflets fail to meet, giving **functional MR** with a **holosystolic apical murmur**. **Diuresis shrinks the ventricle**, so the murmur softens.

idea.rule: Dilated ventricle = stretched annulus = functional mitral regurgitation.
also: Ischemic MR from papillary muscle dysfunction
Improves with afterload reduction
Left atrial enlargement follows
Treat the cardiomyopathy first
